title: HATSouth 2011 and new TESS 2026 data recover the 0.814-day HATS-70 dip; TESS pixels exclude the 23-arcsec Gaia eclipsing binary, leaving HATS-70 or a star 5.7 arcsec south
abstract: A campaign TESS search found a 0.814-day, about 1,000 ppm, V-shaped dip near the A star HATS-70, which has a 12.9 Jupiter-mass brown dwarf on a 1.888-day orbit. We tested the dip with data that earlier studies did not use. HATSouth ground photometry from 2011-2012 shows an 827 ppm dip at the phase that the TESS ephemeris predicts (z = 2.7 against a night-shuffled null). In a pre-registered forward test, our own TESS full-frame photometry of sector 108 (2026) detects 1,083 ppm at 5.1 sigma, 11.5 min from the predicted time. The pre-registered one-pixel aperture of sector 109 did not detect it; post-hoc 2-4 pixel apertures give 3.4-3.9 sigma. Per-pixel dip images from seven TESS sectors reject the Gaia DR3 eclipsing binary 23 arcsec away (delta chi2 = 120) and every catalogued star at 10 arcsec or more. HATS-70 and two G = 19.75 stars at 5.7 and 7.3 arcsec fit equally. The 7.3-arcsec star has normal Gaia flux scatter and cannot have the 51% eclipses it would need. The 5.7-arcsec star has high scatter (96th percentile of controls), which agrees with the 47% eclipses it would need. The mean pixel position is 5 arcsec south-west of HATS-70 (p = 0.04 from on-target injections). The dip-to-transit depth ratio is 0.21 +- 0.02 in all sectors and apertures, and 2011-2026 times fit P = 0.8142612 +- 0.0000020 d. N-body tests show that an on-target planet survives only if the brown-dwarf orbit has e below about 0.05. The source is thus HATS-70 or the 5.7-arcsec star. Seeing-limited photometry at the 184 predicted 2026-2027 times can decide.

TESS pixel localisation: the 23-arcsec Gaia eclipsing binary and all stars beyond 10 arcsec are rejected; HATS-70 and two faint stars at 5.7 and 7.3 arcsec remain.
Gaia G scatter rejects deep eclipses of the 7.3-arcsec star and agrees with about 45% eclipses of the 5.7-arcsec star.

citations.reason: Found the HATS-70 0.814-day signal; we use its residual light curve for the ephemeris and test its blend alternative.
Found a repeat signal in later TESS sectors and asked for a second telescope and localisation; our independent data support the repeat and add both.
